answer.label: Not Hippocrates — a turn-of-the-century medical maxim, in print by 1899
answer.authorDates: Earliest close match spoken by Henry George Plimmer, London, 2 October 1899 · originator unknown
answer.sourceLine: This wording appears in none of the surviving Hippocratic writings. Quote Investigator traces the maxim to turn-of-the-century medical periodicals: the earliest close match is an address by the pathologist Henry George Plimmer, delivered 2 October 1899 and printed in St. Mary’s Hospital Gazette. Woods Hutchinson popularized the saying from 1902 while crediting the Guy’s Hospital physician Walter Moxon — a claim QI could not substantiate — and the only Hippocrates ascription in QI’s chronology is a California newspaper health column of 8 January 1987.

Earliest in QI’s chronology: a health column in the Santa Ynez Valley News (Solvang, California), 8 January 1987

source.excerpt: You will have to acquire, too, for any success to be given you, an accurate knowledge of human nature, and you will find that it is quite as important for the doctor to know what kind of patient the disease has for host, as to know what sort of disease the patient has for guest.
trail: Wikiquote lists the saying in its Disputed section for Hippocrates, noting that an exhaustive 2019 search by Quote Investigator found the earliest close match in 1899 and that “the originator remains unknown.”

Quote Investigator’s earliest strong match is Henry George Plimmer, lecturer on pathology and bacteriology at St Mary’s Hospital Medical School, in an address of 2 October 1899 printed in St. Mary’s Hospital Gazette.

From July 1902 onward Woods Hutchinson repeated the line in the Medical Sentinel, The Lancet, JAMA and The Saturday Evening Post, each time crediting Walter Moxon — who died in 1886, and in whose writings QI has not found it.
The ancient-Greek label is late: the only Hippocrates ascription in QI’s chronology is a 1987 newspaper health column in Solvang, California.
source.excerptNote: Plimmer’s 1899 wording, as transcribed by Quote Investigator from St. Mary’s Hospital Gazette. The familiar modern shape — “It is more important to know what sort of a patient has the disease than what sort of a disease the patient has” — was already being printed without any author, as an “old saw,” in The Journal of the American Medical Association of 12 August 1905.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for this exact wording, because no author or source work has ever been identified for it. The documented forerunners are all safely old — Plimmer’s 1899 address and the anonymous 1905 JAMA version were published long before 1931 and are in the public domain in the United States — and the ancient Hippocratic writings are of course long out of copyright, but this sentence belongs to neither.

author.name: Hippocrates
author.heading: About Hippocrates
author.metaLine: c. 460 – c. 370 BC · Greek physician of Kos, traditionally the “Father of Medicine”
author.bio: Hippocrates of Kos was a Greek physician of the classical period, traditionally called the “Father of Medicine” for separating medicine from superstition and grounding it in observation and prognosis. The treatises of the Hippocratic Corpus carry his name, but very little is known concretely about what he himself thought, wrote or did — which is exactly why modern aphorisms about holistic care attach to him so easily. This is one of them: the sentiment is broadly Hippocratic, the sentence is not.

misattribution.heading: How a Victorian maxim became ancient Greek
misattribution.intro: The saying is real, useful and old — but late-nineteenth-century rather than ancient, and it has collected several different fathers along the way.

items.why: No such sentence appears in the Hippocratic writings, and Wikiquote files it under “Disputed”, noting the originator is unknown. The only Hippocrates credit in Quote Investigator’s chronology is a health column in the Santa Ynez Valley News of Solvang, California, dated 8 January 1987 — and even there the wording ran “I would rather know what sort of person has a disease…”

Woods Hutchinson attributed the “witty paradox” to Moxon from 1902 onward, and most later citations follow him. But Moxon (1836–1886), a physician at Guy’s Hospital in London, died before the first known attribution, and QI found no substantive support for the claim in his writings.

James J. Walsh of Fordham credited “old Dr. Parry of Bath” in 1910 and again in his 1912 book Psychotherapy. Parry died in 1822, and QI treats the long delay before this credit appears as significantly reducing its credibility.

A close variant — “It is much more important to know what sort of a patient has a disease…” — circulates widely under Osler’s name, while this page’s exact wording is the one usually carried under the Hippocrates label. Hutchinson mentioned Osler in The Lancet in January 1903 as one of those who had stressed the point, but credited the phrase to Moxon, not to Osler; Osler’s own 1903 piece in Medical News expressed the idea in quite different words.

misattribution.truthLine: The real story: a medical saying already in circulation by 1899, popularized in British and American journals after 1902 and printed as an anonymous “old saw” by 1905 — with no documented link to Hippocrates at all.

context.heading: Why the line travels
lead: It is the slogan of patient-centred medicine: a one-sentence argument that a fever in one body is not the same illness as a fever in another. Doctors quote it in graduation addresses, textbook prefaces and journal editorials, and the “Hippocrates” label lends a Victorian consulting-room maxim the authority of antiquity.

The record runs the other way. The sentence enters print in English-language medical periodicals at the turn of the twentieth century, in a dozen slightly different shapes — patient or person, kind or sort, “quite as important” or “more important” — the classic signature of a saying passed by ear rather than copied from a text. By August 1905 JAMA could print it with no author at all, calling it simply an “old saw.”
context.detailsSummary: Osler, Moxon, Parry — the three names it collects
detailsBody: A close variant of the line circulates widely under William Osler’s name, but Quote Investigator found no coinage by him: Woods Hutchinson named Osler in The Lancet in January 1903 among physicians who had emphasized the idea, while crediting the phrase itself to Moxon, and Osler’s own 1903 article in Medical News made the point in quite different words.

Walter Moxon (1836–1886), the Guy’s Hospital physician Hutchinson pointed to, died before the earliest known attribution to him, and QI has not located the sentence anywhere in his writings. Caleb Hillier Parry, credited by the medical historian James J. Walsh in 1910, died in 1822 — a delay QI says makes the connection unlikely and significantly reduces the credit’s credibility.

sourcesVerified.claim: Earliest strong match for the maxim is H. G. Plimmer's address of 2 October 1899, printed in St. Mary's Hospital Gazette, London: "it is quite as important for the doctor to know what kind of patient the disease has for host, as to know what sort of disease the patient has for guest."

Woods Hutchinson repeated and popularized the saying from July 1902 (Medical Sentinel), then in The Lancet (Jan 1903), JAMA (Dec 1904) and The Saturday Evening Post (1908), each time crediting Walter Moxon; Moxon died in 1886 and QI found no substantive support for the claim in his writings.

James J. Walsh credited "old Dr. Parry of Bath" (Caleb Hillier Parry) in 1910 (International Clinics) and 1912 (Psychotherapy); Parry died in 1822 and QI says the long delay significantly reduces the credibility of the ascription.

Hutchinson mentioned William Osler in the January 1903 Lancet article but did not credit him with coinage; Osler's own January 1903 Medical News article expressed a similar idea in different phrasing.

The August 12, 1905 JAMA editorial printed "It is more important to know what sort of a patient has the disease than what sort of a disease the patient has" without attribution, labelling it an "old saw".

The Hippocrates ascription in QI's chronology is an 8 January 1987 health column by Dr. Kathie Boisen in the Santa Ynez Valley News (Solvang, California): "I would rather know what sort of person has a disease than what sort of disease a person has."

Wikiquote's Hippocrates page lists "It is quite as important to know what kind of a patient the disease has got, as to know what kind of a disease the patient has got" in its Disputed section, citing QI's 2019 finding that Plimmer's 1899 version is the earliest close match and that "the originator remains unknown."

Hippocrates of Kos, c. 460 - c. 370 BC, Greek physician traditionally called the "Father of Medicine"; the article states very little is known concretely about what Hippocrates himself thought, wrote and did.
Henry George Plimmer (1856/57-1918) was a British doctor and medical researcher in cancer, comparative pathology, bacteriology and parasitology who worked at St Mary's Hospital, London.
Walter Moxon (27 June 1836 - 21 July 1886) was an Irish physician in London associated with Guy's Hospital.

Wikisource's Hippocrates author page hosts English texts of the Hippocratic works (Aphorisms, Of the Epidemics, On Ancient Medicine, the Oath and others) and gives his dates as c. 460 BCE - c. 370 BCE.

The U.S. National Library of Medicine's "Shakespeare and the Four Humors" teacher handout prints the exact wording "It is more important to know what sort of person has a disease than to know what sort of disease a person has" and labels it "commonly attributed to Hippocrates."
